one_liner: Go RPC framework with its own binary TCP protocol and built-in service governance; 2.3-2.6x grpc-go throughput in author's benchmark.
what_it_does: rpcx is a Dubbo-style RPC framework for Go. You register ordinary Go methods of the form Method(ctx, *Args, *Reply) error, with no .proto/IDL required, and call them through an XClient. The XClient adds service discovery (peer-to-peer, fixed server lists, mDNS, DNS, with etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul/Redis registries in separate rpcxio modules), load balancing (random, round-robin, weighted, consistent hash, ping, geo), Failover/Failtry/Failfast, retries, circuit breaking and backup requests. Payloads can be raw bytes, JSON, Protobuf, MessagePack or Thrift over TCP, Unix sockets, HTTP/WebSocket, or QUIC/KCP (behind build tags), with experimental io_uring and RDMA listeners. It is not a drop-in for gRPC: the wire protocol is rpcx-specific, so non-Go callers go through rpcx-gateway (HTTP), the built-in JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint, rpcx-java or rpcx-rs.
how_it_is_fast: Each call is one compact custom frame multiplexed by sequence id over a plain TCP connection. The frame is a 12-byte header (magic byte, version, flag bits, codec byte, 8-byte sequence id) followed by length-prefixed service path, method, metadata and payload, so there is no HTTP/2 framing, HPACK or flow-control windows as in grpc-go. Frames are encoded into size-classed sync.Pool buffers (512 B to 4 KB) and sent with a single conn.Write. Decoded arg/reply structs are recycled through per-type sync.Pools, and each request runs on its own goroutine or, optionally, a pond worker pool (WithPool). In the benchmark both sides used the same gogofaster-generated Protobuf code and 10 pooled client connections, so the gap comes from transport and framework overhead, not the codec.
when_to_use: Go-to-Go services where you own both ends and want more unary RPC throughput than grpc-go for small (~0.5-1 KB) Protobuf messages at 100-5000 concurrent callers.

Teams that want Dubbo-like service governance (registry discovery, weighted/consistent-hash/geo/ping selection, failover, circuit breaking, backup requests) inside the RPC library rather than in a service mesh.
Code-first services: exposing existing Go methods as RPCs without writing .proto files, with the codec (Protobuf, MessagePack, JSON, raw bytes) chosen per client.
High-fan-in servers that care about tail latency: in the author's 2021 run, P99.9 at 5000 callers was 52 ms for rpcx and 294 ms for grpc-go.
Deployments that want to switch transports (TCP, Unix socket, QUIC, KCP, in-process memconn) without changing service code.
when_not_to_use: You need gRPC wire compatibility: grpc-web or browser clients, Envoy/Istio gRPC routing, polyglot clients generated from .proto, or standard gRPC health and reflection tooling. rpcx speaks only its own protocol.

APIs built on typed streaming: rpcx offers one-way calls, server-to-client push on the same connection and a StreamService that hands you a raw net.Conn on a separate port, but nothing like gRPC's typed client, server or bidirectional streams.

You need independently reproduced numbers. Every rpcx vs grpc-go result comes from the rpcx author, and the gap changes a lot between rounds: about 1.5x in 2018 (when Go's net/rpc beat rpcx), grpc-go ahead at some concurrency levels in 2019 and 2020, and 2.3-2.6x in 2021.
Handler-dominated or cross-network workloads: the verified gap is for a near-empty handler over loopback, and real processing time or network round trips shrink the framework's share of latency.
Servers exposed to untrusted peers on default settings: MaxMessageLength and MaxDecompressedLength default to 0 (unlimited), so a peer can force large allocations or gzip bombs before auth runs.

integration.dependencies: About 35 direct Go modules at HEAD, including quic-go, kcp-go, godzie44/go-uring, smallnest/gordma, gogo/protobuf, google.golang.org/protobuf, apache/thrift, vmihailenco/msgpack, tinylib/msgp, go-redis, soheilhy/cmux, alitto/pond, rcrowley/go-metrics and rubyist/circuitbreaker. The etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul and Redis registries are separate rpcxio modules.
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.26 at HEAD (go.mod declares go 1.26.0); the benchmarked rpcx 1.6.5 was built with Go 1.16.6
integration.platforms: Any Go target for TCP/HTTP. The reuseport and Unix-socket listeners are !windows only. The io_uring listener is Linux-only, and the client-side io_uring connection is a stub that falls back to TCP. QUIC, KCP and RDMA are behind build tags, and RDMA needs libibverbs on Linux.
integration.thread_safety: The maintainer calls XClient thread-safe for concurrent Call/Go (issue #362, where race-detector reports on shutdown flags were later fixed). Use one XClient per service. Calls to a server are multiplexed over one connection, and XClientPool/OneClientPool round-robin several clients. Server handlers run concurrently, one goroutine or pool worker per request.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — you can reuse your Protobuf message types as args and replies, but services must be rewritten as Method(ctx, *Args, *Reply) error, clients must move to XClient, and rpcx is not wire-compatible with gRPC clients or servers.

gotchas: client.DefaultOption uses MessagePack, not Protobuf. The benchmark explicitly set option.SerializeType = protocol.ProtoBuffer. Plain structs under the default go through reflection-based vmihailenco/msgpack unless you generate tinylib/msgp code.

Arg and reply objects that implement Reset() (every generated Protobuf message does) are reset and returned to a sync.Pool as soon as the handler returns. Do not keep them or hand them to other goroutines.
Message size and decompressed size are unlimited by default. Set WithMaxMessageLength and WithMaxDecompressedLength on any server that accepts untrusted traffic.

APIs have churned. The 2021 benchmark server sets server.UsePool, which does not exist at HEAD (the pool is now the WithPool option, added in 1.8.0), and the etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul plugins moved to separate modules in 1.7-1.8, so older tutorials' imports break. The README names the stable branch as both v1.7.x and v1.9.4, and open issue #945 reports that six example links on the official site 404 because they point at a main branch instead of master.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick rpcx over Kitex (the other Go framework here) if you want a standard-netpoller Go stack with registry-based governance built in. In rpcx's own 2021 run, Kitex 0.0.3 reached 178-213k TPS with P99.9 up to 1,081 ms at 5000 clients, against 249-318k TPS and 52 ms for rpcx; current Kitex was not tested. Choose wtx or grpcxx instead if you must keep the gRPC wire protocol, and cmd-stream-go if you want a lean Go command transport (benchmarked at 1-16 clients) rather than a full microservice framework.
verified_claims_summary: The rpcx author's 2021 benchmark ran over loopback (Go 1.16.6, 2x Xeon Silver 4110, 32 threads), with 10M requests per run and 100-5000 concurrent callers sharing 10 client connections. rpcx 1.6.5 echoed a 581-byte gogofaster Protobuf message at 249-318k TPS, against 96-136k for grpc-go 1.39.0 (2.3-2.6x) and 189-219k for Go's net/rpc (1.3-1.5x), and at 5000 callers its mean/P99.9 latency was 15/52 ms against grpc-go's 40/294 ms. Earlier rounds by the same author show a smaller or reversed gap, and no independent reproduction was found.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-03, tag v1.9.4, 8.3k stars, 4 open issues) and licensed Apache-2.0: GitHub's API says NOASSERTION, but the file is the standard Apache 2.0 text. It is an ordinary Go module, though HEAD now needs Go 1.26.
